corrected_proposal.title: DOGE Lease List Targets 47 SSA Sites; SSA Says Most Were Unstaffed Hearing Rooms
corrected_proposal.description_short: AP reported 47 SSA locations on a lease-cancellation list, with 26 listed for 2025; SSA said most were unstaffed hearing rooms.
corrected_proposal.description_medium: AP reported March 19 that DOGE’s lease-cancellation list included 47 SSA locations, with 26 expected to close during 2025. On March 27, SSA said no local field office had been permanently closed or announced for closure since January 1, and said most listed sites were unstaffed hearing rooms. The record supports a planned lease action, not the original claim that 600 field offices closed or a documented loss of service.
corrected_proposal.description_long: On March 19, 2025, the Associated Press reported that DOGE had listed 47 Social Security Administration offices for lease cancellation and that 26 entries were expected to close during the year, based on General Services Administration data. This was a plan tied to lease terminations, not proof that 47 public field offices had permanently closed. SSA responded on March 27 that no local field office had been permanently closed or announced for permanent closure since January 1. The agency said most sites identified to GSA were small hearing rooms without assigned employees; it separately said it had announced closure of one hearing office in White Plains, New York. The available records support a proposed lease-termination effort at SSA locations, with facility types and dates varying across the list. They do not support the original claim that about 600 of roughly 1,200 field offices were closed. The sources reviewed also do not establish that every lease cancellation occurred or quantify resulting service loss, delays, or harm to claimants. This entry records the plan and the agency’s contemporaneous correction; outcomes at individual locations remain uncertain.

corrected_proposal.title: Trump Uses “Animals” Remark During California Immigration Roundtable
corrected_proposal.description_short: Trump Used “Animals” Remark During May 2018 California Immigration Roundtable
corrected_proposal.description_medium: At a May 16, 2018, White House roundtable on sanctuary-city policies, President Donald Trump said, “These aren’t people. These are animals” after Fresno County Sheriff Margaret Mims said she knew of an MS-13 member she could not report to ICE. Trump’s reply referred broadly to “people coming into the country” without naming a group. The White House and Trump later said he meant MS-13; FactCheck.org said the original remark’s intended target could not be established with certainty.
corrected_proposal.description_long: On May 16, 2018, President Donald Trump held a White House roundtable with California mayors, sheriffs and other officials about sanctuary-city policies. During the discussion, Fresno County Sheriff Margaret Mims said she knew of an MS-13 member but could not tell ICE unless that person met a threshold. Trump replied that “people coming into the country” were “animals,” saying, “These aren’t people. These are animals.” In the official transcript, the remark immediately follows Mims’s reference to MS-13, but Trump’s reply does not name the gang. The White House press secretary later said Trump was referring to MS-13 gang members, and Trump said the next day that he meant MS-13. FactCheck.org reported those explanations while noting that it could not determine exactly what Trump meant in the original remark. The record should therefore describe the words and their immediate setting, then attribute the later clarification separately. It should not say the transcript proves that Trump was referring to all immigrants, or that it definitively proves he meant only MS-13. The sources establish the public remark and context; they do not document a resulting policy change or quantify harm caused by it.

corrected_proposal.title: Trump Acknowledged Istanbul Business Conflict in 2015 Interview
corrected_proposal.description_short: Trump said a major Istanbul building gave him “a little conflict of interest” when discussing Turkey in a 2015 interview.
corrected_proposal.description_medium: In a December 1, 2015 interview on Breitbart News Daily, Donald Trump said he had “a little conflict of interest” because of a major building in Istanbul called Trump Towers. This supports a public acknowledgment of a potential business conflict while discussing Turkey. It does not establish repeated Turkish-government bookings at the Istanbul property or that the business interest shaped U.S. policy toward Turkey.
corrected_proposal.description_long: On December 1, 2015, Donald Trump spoke on Breitbart News Daily about Turkey and said he had “a little conflict of interest” because he had a major building in Istanbul called Trump Towers. TIME later quoted the remark and identified it as a 2015 interview; Politico reported on a Tuesday-morning Breitbart interview on December 1, 2015. The statement documents a public acknowledgment of a potential business conflict while discussing Turkey. It does not show that Turkish government agencies or affiliated groups booked Trump Towers Istanbul during his presidency, that those bookings generated payments to Trump, or that U.S. decisions toward Turkey were made to benefit the property. The held record further alleges that Trump repeatedly favored President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan because of this business interest. The sources accessed for this repair do not establish that causal link. This account therefore records the 2015 statement and leaves the broader booking and policy-influence allegations unresolved; it does not present them as findings of corruption or proof that the property changed government policy.
corrected_proposal.date_precision: Politico reports the Breitbart interview on December 1, 2015; TIME independently dates the quoted interview to 2015.
